name: Sapphire (Crayola)
lede: Sapphire (Crayola) is a mid, slightly violet blue from Crayola's color list, almost indistinguishable from the company's own B'dazzled Blue.

sections.title: A qualified name in the Crayola list
sections.body:
Wikipedia lists Sapphire as a Crayola color at #2D5DA1, citing the company directly [1]. Our library files it among the "obscure, qualified or novelty" names, since nobody reaches for plain *sapphire* the way they do for *blue* or *navy*; the qualifier "(Crayola)" is doing real work [1].

In ISCC-NBS terms it falls in block 182, "moderate blue," with a looser-than-usual match, ΔE 5.2, and its Munsell notation is 5.7PB 3.9/10.0 [2]. Our graph files it, along with [[cerulean-blue|Cerulean Blue]] and [[marine|Marine]], under the general Blues family [2].

sections.title: Its nearest neighbors
sections.body:
The closest everyday name in our library is [[denim]], about 3.7 units away [1]. Closer still is Crayola's own [[b-dazzled-blue|B'dazzled Blue]], a separate crayon-box name for an almost identical blue, about 2.2 units off [3].

The mineral-named [[sapphire-blue|Sapphire Blue]] is a different color: lighter and more saturated, documented in Ridgway's 1912 plates and the 1955 ISCC-NBS list rather than in any crayon box [2][3]. The two "Sapphire" names share only a gemstone, not a common source [2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a match for this blue in 53 of 23,781 paintings, 0.22 percent, as photographed; a tighter within-painting read narrows that to 36 [4]. That makes it rarer than about 55 percent of the named colors we track [4].

It peaks in paintings from the 1900s decade, found in 0.5 percent of the 1,674 paintings on file from then, about 2.5 times the rate its neighbors get [4]. Within a painting it most often plays an accent, in 67 percent of its 36 appearances [4]. The earliest match on file is a 1426 panel by [[painter:fra-angelico|Fra Angelico]], though the archive's early centuries are thin, so that is a floor, not a first date [4].
